lines.text: This is the North Sea, higher than about a quarter of it.
And this is how the Dutch keep them apart.
So why build a country below the sea? Nobody did. It sank.
A thousand years ago, the west was soggy peat. Farmers drained it, and drained peat shrinks.
So the land dropped, needed more draining, and dropped again.
Dikes ringed the fields, and windmills pumped them dry.
Today, the lowest point is almost seven metres below sea level.
In 1932, a thirty-two kilometre dam sealed off an entire inland sea.
Behind it, they pumped the seabed dry, and built a province on it.
Then in 1953, a storm surge broke the dikes in the southwest. Over eighteen hundred people died.
The answer was the Delta Works: dams and barriers across the estuaries.
The largest stays open for the tides, and drops sixty-two steel gates in a storm.
None of it is finished. The land is still sinking, and the sea is rising.
Holding the line is a job that never ends.
